title: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three doshas as a way of noticing, and Sushruta's word for well: svastha, a definition that ends in a clear, content mind.

Early morning, the body is slow to get going, and the snooze button looks very reasonable. Around noon, hunger gets sharp, and so does the temper. Late afternoon, attention starts to scatter like leaves in a parking lot. A day has moods, and they tend to arrive roughly on schedule. The Ashtanga Hridaya noticed a pattern like that too. It doesn't hand out a timetable to the minute. It gives each part of the day a dosha.

In paraphrase, the verse says this. The doshas run through the whole body, and they rise in turn: kapha at the beginning, pitta in the middle, vata at the end. The beginning, middle and end of what? Of a life, of a day, of a night, and of a meal. One three-part pattern, laid over four clocks. Take the day: at its beginning kapha, the heavy, slow, steady one; in the middle pitta, the hot and sharp; toward the end vata, the light and moving. Over a life it reads the same way: kapha in childhood, pitta in the middle years, vata in old age. Over a meal: heaviness right after eating, then the heat of digestion, then lightness. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It gives no exact hours; beginning, middle and end are all it offers, and how anyone divides those up is a later question. And notice the tone. The doshas are simply taking turns, the way the light changes across a day. That's the gift for noticing. A slow morning may not be a character flaw. A sharp noon may not be a personal failing. Some of it may be the hour. On this path, that's a way of looking, not a rule to live by, and never a diagnosis. Anything about sleep or energy that keeps on is a question for a doctor.

segments.voice: Notice what part of the day it is right now: beginning, middle or end. Then look for that part's quality in your body: heaviness, heat, or lightness and a skittering mind. Don't judge what you find; just notice whether the hour and the body agree today, or rest in prayer if you pray.
The three doshas, as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. Today, on the clock: kapha at the beginning, pitta in the middle, vata at the end.
